headlines.article_text: Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in bonds, it said in a filing. The plans were outlined last week at its investor day. In this article ORCL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The Oracle logo is displayed on a building at an Oracle campus on September 10, 2025 in Redwood Shores, California. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout. The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week , shares tumbled more than 6% Monday. "This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it." Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments. Oracle's one-day performance The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion. "This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday. Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028. Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.267%. The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 296, up 270% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan. Oracle's five-year credit default swaps on Nov. 2, 2026 While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of August 31, with the bulk in senior notes. What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday. "Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out." — CNBC's Ari Levy contributed reporting. headlines.article_text: Marvell to buy Lumentum in all-stock deal Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Marvell will acquire Lumentum in an all-stock transaction. The deal will expand Marvell's push into optical connectivity for artificial intelligence data centers. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026. In this article MRVL LITE Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:41 04:41 Marvell CEO Matt Murphy on Lumentum deal: We're creating the 'category leader in AI connectivity' Squawk on the Street Marvell Technology 's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday. "You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," he told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here." Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release. Marvell shares slumped 8% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank 13%. Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models. "We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy said. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending. This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology. Marvell 's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies. In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers. "This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them." Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. headlines.article_text: Apple Q4 2026 earnings live updates: Ternus' first call Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu watch now VIDEO 3:49 03:49 Needham's Laura Martin on Apple: 'We need to watch what's happening in China' Squawk on the Street Apple reports fiscal fourth-quarter earnings after the bell on Monday, with new CEO John Ternus expected to address Wall Street in a meaningful way for the first time. Here's what analysts are expecting, according to LSEG. EPS: $1.99 Revenue: $113.39 billion Revenue is expected to increase 11% from $102.5 billion a year earlier. Analysts project $56.59 billion in iPhone sales for the quarter. Wall Street is closely watching iPhone revenue because the report will include eight days of new iPhone 18 Pro sales. But Apple's new flagship device, the iPhone Duo, didn't hit store shelves until the quarter was over, and Apple didn't announce a new entry-level iPhone 18. Apple also raised prices on iPhones by $100, which may have hurt demand in the quarter. Monday's earnings call, set to start at 5 p.m. ET, will be the first with Ternus at the helm. Investors want to hear from him about the company's plans in China after its AI software got approved, as well as the slew of recent product launches and how the company continues to grapple with global shortages of memory and flash storage. Read more CNBC Apple news Apple brings touch to the Mac, ending decades-old stance on touchscreen laptops Apple stock has become an anti-AI trade. Here’s why Apple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens 34 Min Ago Tough market for smartphones and PCs due to memory shortage watch now VIDEO 6:17 06:17 Intel faces a 'multi-quarter' issue balancing PC weakness with AI data-center gains: Vivek Arya Squawk Box Apple is competing in a smartphone and PC market that has "never been worse," IDC's Ryan Reith told CNBC. Consumer electronics companies everywhere are grappling with surging prices for computer parts, including memory and flash storage that's used in every smartphone and laptop. Intel on Friday had its worst day on the stock market since the 1970s, dropping 29%, after the company cited PC softness for a disappointing forecast . Many companies have responded to component shortages by raising prices or reducing specifications for current devices. Consumers are holding onto their old computers for far longer, driving sales down. IDC says the smartphone market is set to drop nearly 17% this year based on shipments. PCs could be down 11%. Apple isn't immune. The company raised prices on almost all of its products since executives warned over the summer that the market was in a "thousand year flood." — Kif Leswing 1 Hour Ago No iPhone Duo this quarter, but some iPhone 18 sales watch now VIDEO 2:07 02:07 Apple ramps iPhone Duo production as early screen failures emerge Squawk Box Asia Apple's new $2,000 foldable phone won't have any sales for the quarter, which ended last month. While Apple and Ternus announced new iPhones on Sept. 9, the foldable Duo didn't go on sale until a month later, on Oct 23. Some analysts have theorized that Apple's most committed fans may have been waiting to see the Duo come out before buying it. There will be a few weeks of sales from the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which went on sale on Sept. 18. — Kif Leswing 3 Hours Ago Ternus has been everywhere John Ternus, chief executive officer of Apple Inc., speaks during an event in Los Angeles, California, US, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Kyle Grillot | Bloomberg | Getty Images Apple investors and customers are still getting to know Ternus, but since he took over for Tim Cook on Sept. 1, the new CEO has embraced his new role as the face of the iPhone company. Ternus' first major appearance came nine days into his tenure, when he unveiled the iPhone Duo at Apple's headquarters. A week later, he was walking the red carpet at the Emmys. He then flew to New York, where he opened the doors at an Apple store to commemorate the new iPhone Pro going on sale. He also went to Austin, Texas, this month to kick off sales of the iPhone Duo, and appeared at an elementary school and an F1 race while on the trip. And he's had a busy media schedule, including an appearance on the cover of Time magazine. Last week, Ternus continued a new style of Apple product introduction in unveiling the first MacBook with a touchscreen using a format he first tried out in the spring. That's when Apple launched its low-cost MacBook Neo. Ternus addressed a crowd of media and analysts, giving a five minute speech interspersed with a few short videos. Investors will get their first in-depth look at Ternus on Monday. He's been on the past few calls, but hasn't given extended remarks, and largely deferred to Cook when asked questions. — Kif Leswing 3 Hours Ago Stock is Wall Street's favorite among the megacaps Apple vs. Nasdaq this year Heading into its earnings report, Apple has emerged as the preferred megacap tech stock on Wall Street. The shares are up 27% this year as of Friday's close, by far outpacing Apple's leading peers. It's also the last among the group (other than Nvidia, which reports next month) to issue quarterly earnings. Investors weren't kind to the hyperscalers over the past two weeks, scrutinizing their hefty expenses and dwindling cash flows. Apple is in a much different category as the iPhone maker has avoided running up huge capital expenditures bills, taking a more measured approach to its AI investing. —Ari Levy
